name: Classical radicalism
summary: Classical radicalism was the leftward wing of liberalism from the late eighteenth to the mid-nineteenth century, centred on Britain. It demanded a far wider franchise, frequent elections and secret ballot, the end of hereditary monarchy, aristocratic privilege and sinecures, freedom of the press, secular or disestablished churches, free trade and cheaper government, and legal and penal reform on rational or utilitarian grounds.
scope: British radicalism c.1780-1870: Paine's Rights of Man, the philosophic radicals (Bentham, James Mill, their circle, with J.S. Mill's liberty doctrine), the Manchester free-traders (Cobden, Bright) and Chartist demands for wider suffrage. Excludes the French Radical Party of 1901 and later socialist or social-liberal radicalism.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Paine
keyFigures.role: Author of Rights of Man, the foundational radical case against hereditary government.

keyFigures.name: Jeremy Bentham
keyFigures.role: Founder of utilitarianism and leading figure of the philosophic radicals.

keyFigures.name: James Mill
keyFigures.role: Bentham's chief disciple, who argued for representative democracy and wider suffrage.

sources.title: Radicals (UK)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Anti-Corn Law League, ballot and suffrage agitation, Chartism, nonconformist and disestablishment demands, slimmed-down executive.

universal-healthcare.rationale: No state health service existed in the period; inferred from the radical priority on poor relief and the reformist, utilitarian stress on general welfare, as in Paine's tax-funded relief proposals.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage-fixing by law was anachronistic and clashed with the political-economy outlook of Ricardo and the Mills, though Paine-style relief for the poor pulled the other way.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Philosophic radicals drew on Ricardian political economy and the Manchester radicals attacked protection and monopoly, so markets were generally trusted over aristocratic state interference.

public-ownership.rationale: Modern utilities did not exist; radicals distrusted self-interested governments and sought a slimmed-down executive, so large state ownership was not a programme item.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Paine proposed a progressive tax on large estates reaching twenty shillings in the pound at the top, and radicals sought to cut aristocratic privilege, though many mainstream radicals mainly wanted lower taxes overall.

unions-good.rationale: Radicals such as Place campaigned for the right to combine, but philosophic radicals and Manchester liberals were wary of union wage-setting; adherents were split.

property-fundamental.rationale: Radicals defended keeping the fruits of one's labor and Paine counts property among retained rights, but they also attacked feudal landed privilege and primogeniture, so it is not an override-proof right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporations in the modern sense were not the target; radicals opposed monopolies and chartered privilege yet favoured free enterprise, leaving no clear stance.

cut-welfare.rationale: Paine wanted to replace poor-rates with direct grants to the poor, while Benthamites backed the harsh 1834 Poor Law; radicals were mixed, with the humanitarian strand dominating on principle.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Inferred from the radical defence of free press and speech against state repression and from distrust of rulers' self-interest.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred from J.S. Mill's harm principle, which rules out restricting adults for their own good; drugs were not a period issue.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Radicals defended a free press and free speech against censorship, and Mill's harm principle rejects restriction for mere offence.

strong-leader.rationale: Radicals sought representative, accountable government with frequent elections and rejected single rulers who could exploit subjects.

state-harmful.rationale: Radicals wanted a reformed, accountable and limited state, not its abolition; Mill called representative government the great modern discovery.

limit-guns.rationale: Not addressed; radicals favoured citizen militia ideas yet also public order, so adherents would split.

empower-police-military.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and sought cuts in armies and taxation; Paine proposed reducing the army and navy.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Inferred from Mill's harm principle on self-regarding conduct; the issue was not discussed in the period sources used.

decide-locally.rationale: Radicals favoured both wide representative democracy and reform of local corporations; no settled stance on subsidiarity.

rehabilitation.rationale: James Mill's work on prisons treated punishment as remedial education to reform character, and Benthamite penal reform aimed at deterrence and reform rather than cruelty.

traditional-family.rationale: Radicals rejected inherited authority in general and Mill later attacked sex-based subordination, though the family was not a central target.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the harm principle and the radical drift toward equal rights, though period radicals largely did not address it.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred from utilitarian and harm-principle reasoning; not addressed in the period.

more-religion-public.rationale: Radicals favoured secularism and anti-clericalism and sought to end church privileges, with Paine insisting religion should not be a state political tool.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Radicals backed anti-slavery, but active programmes to correct historical racial injustice are anachronistic and not documented.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Mill held that character is formed by circumstance and Thompson attacked the subjection of women, but the modern formulation is anachronistic.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Radicalism's civic nationalism and rationalism put reform and universal principles ahead of inherited tradition.

gradual-change.rationale: Radicals sought radical reform of the electoral and legal system and attacked inherited institutions; Paine denied that past generations bind the living.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Inferred from the radical opposition to protection and privilege and from Paine's cosmopolitan view of commerce and a European republic; period immigration controls were not a platform issue.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Paine imagined a European republic and radicals favoured peace, but no international bodies existed; inferred, with no clear stance.

free-trade.rationale: The Manchester radicals Cobden and Bright led the Anti-Corn Law League against grain duties, and Paine praised commerce as a pacific system that makes nations useful to each other.

nation-first.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and internationalist in outlook, with Paine hoping for peace between nations; mild inference.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Radicals backed liberty abroad but the Manchester wing opposed foreign wars and spending; adherents were split.

open-borders.rationale: Paine's cosmopolitan language suggests sympathy, but open borders as a programme was not advanced; split.

limit-growth.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals backed commerce and economic growth through free trade.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic and not inferable from stated principles.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Rationalism and faith in reform and reason were typical of the tradition, though technology was not a stated theme.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing in the principles decides it.

revolution-justified.rationale: Paine defended the French revolt against hereditary despotism, while the philosophic radicals worked through lobbying and feared revolutionary excess, so the strands differ.

experts-over-public.rationale: Radicals extended the franchise and held that rulers' interests diverge from the governed, so expertise could not replace democratic accountability; Bentham's technocratic streak makes it mild.

central-planning.rationale: Radical political economy (Ricardo, Mill) and the Manchester men favoured exchange and attacked state-granted privilege.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not discussed in the classical period; J.S. Mill later sympathised with cooperatives, but the mainstream did not address it.

land-value-tax.rationale: Ricardian rent theory made land taxation attractive to some radicals, but replacing most taxes with it was a later Georgist idea.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Paine's progressive estate tax and abolition of primogeniture aimed to break up large holdings, and radicals attacked inherited privilege.

basic-income.rationale: Paine's grants to children, the old and new mothers resemble it, but unconditional universal income was not proposed.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The Anti-Corn Law League and the Manchester radicals attacked tariffs as favouring landowners at consumers' expense.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Radicals sought a slimmed-down executive and opposed state-granted privilege and monopoly.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Paine's tax scheme and attack on primogeniture were designed to divide large estates, and radicals sought wider property ownership against aristocratic land concentration.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not a classical radical aim; the tradition accepted market exchange and wages.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Banking policy was debated among radicals (Cobbett attacked paper money) but not as an agreed position.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognised bodies setting wages are contrary to liberal-radical individualism and political economy.

one-party-rule.rationale: Radicals demanded wide suffrage, frequent elections and free press; single-party rule contradicts representative government.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Paine condemned hereditary monarchy as despotism, James Mill rejected monarchy as exploitable, and republicanism is listed among radical positions.

democracy-best.rationale: Radicals favoured democratic accountability, though James Mill and Bentham worried about interest and J.S. Mill later weighted votes; the core is pro-democracy.

direct-votes.rationale: Direct democracy is listed among radical associations, but the philosophic radicals prized representative government as the grand modern discovery; split.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils replacing parliaments are alien to a tradition that built on parliamentary reform and wider suffrage.

right-to-secede.rationale: Inferred from consent doctrine, but radicals were not concerned with secession in sources used.

natural-rulers.rationale: Paine said all men are born equal with equal natural right and condemned hereditary government; Mill rejected ruling elites.

political-violence-never.rationale: Philosophic radicals avoided violence and feared revolutionary excess, whereas Paine and Chartists accepted force in extremity; mostly not an absolute rule.

war-builds-character.rationale: Paine wrote he wished war might never exist, and radicals were antimilitarist.

separate-church-state.rationale: Secularism, anti-clericalism and disestablishment were radical causes, and Paine treated religion as a private right.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Rationalism and secularism led radicals to ground law in utility and reason; Paine and Bentham attacked religious authority over government.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Radicals sought reformed public law (Bentham's law reform) and did not propose privatised defence; inferred.

military-superiority.rationale: Antimilitarism and calls for reduced armies and navies, and for lower taxes, were radical themes.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Radical nationalism was civic, and Paine's principles rest on equal rights of all men.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Radicals saw conflict between rulers and ruled, aristocracy versus people, but not Marxist class struggle as history's motor; Chartists were more class-conscious.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Radicals added equality to liberal rights, but of rights and opportunity and ending privilege, not equal outcomes; Paine's grants were minimal relief.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals criticised empire and slavery but did not discuss reparations.

civilizational-union.rationale: Religious or civilizational unions run against secular, civic outlook; inferred.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Bentham and James Mill held that people pursue their own pleasure and designed institutions around it; calling it morally good is more utilitarian than selfish, and J.S. Mill rejected the egoism.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Radicals started from natural and equal individual rights, as in Paine.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Not addressed; utilitarian focus on human happiness suggests no, but no stated stance.

limit-population.rationale: Malthusian ideas split radicals: Place promoted birth control, while Paine-style and Cobbett views differed.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Radicals welcomed commerce and industry, with free-trade manufacturers (the Manchester men) at the forefront.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Radicals favoured progress but also gradual legislation and did not endorse disruption for its own sake.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic, and nothing in the tradition's principles speaks to bodily enhancement either way.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals insisted on democratic accountability of rulers.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Inferred from distrust of state power and defence of free communication of ideas.

restore-past-order.rationale: Radicals attacked inherited institutions; Paine rejected governing from the grave and prized the present generation's authority.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Utilitarian philosophic radicals judged institutions by their consequences for happiness, a strongly results-oriented outlook.

direct-action.rationale: Philosophic radicals worked through lobbying and parliament; the Chartist mass demonstrations also petitioned parliament, though some wings used physical force.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Contrary to the commerce and progress orientation of the tradition.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Ricardian political economy accepted specialisation and exchange.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Classical radicals thought people should keep the fruits of their labor; Paine's grants were targeted relief.

production-for-use.rationale: A socialist formulation; classical radicals accepted market production, inferred.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Radicals attacked aristocratic and rentier privilege more than industrial profit, and Ricardian economics did not treat profit as exploitation; some labour radicals differed.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Incompatible with the radical demand for wide suffrage and representative accountability.

collective-farming.rationale: Radicals aimed at dividing landed estates among many owners, not collectivisation.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Cobden and Bright argued commerce promotes peace and Paine called it pacific, which is the opposite thesis; but critics of empire among radicals also blamed arms and aristocracy.

taxation-theft.rationale: Radicals accepted taxation, wanting it lower and fairer, and Paine proposed tax-funded relief.

harm-principle.rationale: J.S. Mill's harm principle is the classic statement within the tradition, though earlier radicals such as Bentham reasoned from utility instead.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Radicals championed individual rights, but groups such as nonconformists and women received claims and Bentham called natural rights nonsense; split.

conscription.rationale: Antimilitarism suggests opposition; some radicals favoured citizen militias, so not strong.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Radicals made the vote the central check, with frequent elections to align rulers' interests with the people's.

state-as-business.rationale: Radicals sought accountable government of the people, not customer-service governance.

positive-liberty.rationale: Radicalism added social and educational reform to liberal rights, but positive-liberty theory is later; Mill's education stress points mildly toward it.

media-academia-power.rationale: Radicals regarded the press as a check on rulers, but not as the true power over elected officials.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Radicals held that character is formed by circumstances and that all men are equal; racial hierarchy was contrary to Paine's principles.

organic-representation.rationale: Radicals favoured representation of individuals by equal suffrage, against corporate and hereditary bodies.

total-state.rationale: Radicals sought a limited, accountable executive and free expression (s2, s5), the opposite of a state directing every area of life; totalitarianism is not discussed directly.

national-rebirth.rationale: Radicals sought reform of institutions via reason, not mythic national regeneration.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Antimilitarism and the Manchester opposition to costly foreign adventures.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Feudal oaths of loyalty are not discussed; rejection is inferred from Paine's government by consent and equal rights.

bound-labor.rationale: Paine's principle that no generation or man has property in man; radicals attacked feudal privilege and backed anti-slavery.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Rationalism and Enlightenment confidence in reason as the guide to truth.

universal-morality.rationale: Radicals relied on reason and universal principles (equal natural rights, utility), with J.S. Mill adding qualifications.

single-common-good.rationale: Utilitarians aimed at the greatest happiness, but also argued rulers' interests diverge from the governed and so built institutions to balance interests; split.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Democratic accountability was a political principle; workplace extension was a later (Mill's cooperatives, Owenite) idea not shared by the mainstream.

school-vouchers.rationale: Radicals prized education, with divisions over state versus voluntary provision; vouchers not discussed.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Early radicals sought lower taxes and economy in government, and Paine proposed cutting spending, though Keynesian stimulus is anachronistic.

economic-freedom.rationale: Radicals tied political liberty to free trade and property, but mainly argued from political reform; inferred.

rule-by-example.rationale: Radicals relied on laws, institutions and accountability rather than rulers' virtue, assuming rulers pursue self-interest.

national-self-determination.rationale: Civic nationalism and support for liberal revolutions such as Belgium's and the 1848 uprisings.

force-without-un.rationale: Anachronistic; antimilitarism and Manchester non-intervention suggest caution.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Rationalism is a defining radical trait, and Paine's Rights of Man names reason as the only legitimate source of government against superstition and power.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Radicals never debated limiting welfare by citizenship; Paine's relief scheme was framed for the poor generally.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Benthamite poor-law reformers favoured work conditions, while Paine's grants were unconditional except schooling; split.

class-collaboration.rationale: Middle-class radicals stressed shared interest against landlords, while working-class radicals saw conflict; split.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Anachronistic futurist stance; radicals attacked institutions of privilege, not libraries.

dominated-front.rationale: Anachronistic anti-Western front; inferred from internationalism.

workers-nation.rationale: Radicalism focused on nationwide political reform and Paine imagined a broader republic; anachronistic.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: James Mill excluded women from the vote on the basis of household interest, but Thompson and J.S. Mill criticised it; on balance reformers moved toward equality.

ban-interest.rationale: Political economy of Bentham (his defence of usury) and Ricardo favoured free lending.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Radicals argued from equal natural rights and many campaigned against slavery (s4, s5), which runs against racial classification in law; segregation is not discussed directly.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Radicals argued that rulers use government for their own interests, which resembles this, but no class theory; split by wording.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Anachronistic energy-policy question with no radical position; nothing in the principles decides it.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Civic nationalism and tolerance of nonconformity suggest rejecting forced assimilation; inferred.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy claim foreign to rationalist radicalism.

proportional-representation.rationale: J.S. Mill backed proportional representation (Hare), but most radicals sought equal districts and the ballot; split.

national-mission.rationale: Radicals backed liberal revolutions but opposed costly interventions, with Paine hoping republics would spread by example.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Mill's later writings point to yes and Thompson's Appeal attacked women's exclusion, but the early philosophic radicals denied it.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Radicalism arose against rotten boroughs, sinecures and aristocratic misrule, and Bentham and Mill held rulers pursue their own interest.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Contrary to equal rights and the harm principle.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Inferred from radical demand for accountable rulers and Paine's critique of war making.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Manchester radicals sought a slimmed state, while Benthamites favoured active legal and administrative reform; split.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: No radical source discusses marriage across racial lines; opposition is inferred from their equal natural rights.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Paine states that all men are born equal with equal natural right, and radicals pressed for equality before the law.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Not addressed in the sources used.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Radicals sought equal rights regardless of religion, including admission of nonconformists to office.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Paine treated religion as a retained natural right, and radicals sought toleration and freedom of conscience.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Religious prohibitions imposed by law conflict with secular utilitarian reasoning.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Inferred from secularism and anti-clericalism, though educational policy divided radicals and nonconformists on religious teaching.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Paine holds that legitimate government rests on the people and that government is for the living.

trade-surplus.rationale: The Manchester radicals of the Anti-Corn Law League (s5) attacked protection and mercantilist trade policy, which aimed at an export surplus; the surplus target is not discussed in those words.

population-transfer.rationale: The sources never discuss expelling minorities; opposition is inferred from Paine's equal rights and government by consent.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Free-trade radicals prized competition, but did not make struggle between peoples the engine of progress; split.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Defence of a free press and expression suggests opposing bans; Mill's harm principle similarly.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Radicals opposed aggressive war, but accepted state coercion through taxes and law.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Paine's attack on hereditary power, called slavery, and radical concern with rulers' arbitrary power match it.

separated-powers.rationale: Paine defended constitutions as limits on government, while philosophic radicals chiefly relied on accountable legislature; mild.

vanguard-party.rationale: Foreign to a tradition built on mass reform movements and parliamentary pressure.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Paine's tax-funded relief for the poor, and radical attacks on privilege, point to yes; Manchester strand less so.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Anachronistic, since council housing did not exist; wide small property ownership is the only distant link.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Place and radicals fought combination laws, but political economists doubted union effects.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Malthusians such as James Mill and Ricardo's circle accepted it, but Paine and Cobbett blamed institutions; split.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Radicals sought toleration of nonconformists and civic nationalism.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Radicals relied on elections to align interests; lottery was not a program.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Radicals fought repression of press and assembly, and trusted no ruler with unchecked power.

party-controls-media.rationale: Radicals defended freedom of the press against censorship.

party-commands-army.rationale: Contrary to accountable constitutional government and antimilitarism.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Inferred from civic nationalism and cosmopolitan outlook.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: The Chartist Six Points included payment of MPs, but pay at workers' level is not documented.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Radicals prized independent representatives accountable to voters, not party discipline.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Paine imagined a European republic but supranational union is anachronistic.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Radicals rejected hereditary or executive prerogative, wanting the legislature to control government.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Anti-clerical and disestablishmentarian radicals opposed privileged episcopal establishment.

clerical-rule.rationale: Radicals campaigned against the established church's political privileges and for secular government (s1), which rules out clergy holding supreme power.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Radicals opposed war, but wishing defeat is a Leninist formula.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Radicals defended free press and free expression; Mill rejects moralistic restriction.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Radicals wanted frequent elections and short terms to align interests.

recall-officials.rationale: Frequent elections were the radical method; recall specifically was not stated.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Cobden-style non-intervention and calls to reduce armaments suggest support; inferred.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Contrary to property and market outlook.

people-in-arms.rationale: Some radicals, Paine among those wanting cut armies, favoured militias; not documented as a core position.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Cobbett idealised rural life, whereas manufacturing radicals championed towns; split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: No stated radical position on reunifying divided nations; consent and self-determination give only weak guidance.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Radicals prized education and reason; hostility to educated classes was not a theme.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Radicals held universal rational standards, but opposed hierarchy of peoples; split.

death-penalty.rationale: Benthamite penal reform emphasised reform and proportion, tending toward limiting capital punishment; gravest-crime exceptions were accepted by some.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Inferred from rationalist educational reform and Place-style radicalism; anachronistic.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Rationalism and secularism oppose religious dogma in schooling.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Inferred from free-expression and harm-principle commitments.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Civic nationalism suggests territorial or consent-based citizenship.

minority-language-support.rationale: Not discussed by classical radicals, whose concerns were franchise and privilege rather than language policy.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Radicals sought toleration and the admission of nonconformists, supporting accommodation of conscience; exemptions from general laws are not documented.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: J.S. Mill valued a large variety of characters and lifestyles and tied liberty to individuality.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Anachronistic; the tradition respected contracts and property.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Not a classical radical theme; the tradition sought political and legal reform rather than economic transformation.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Paine defines a constitution as antecedent to government and made by the people.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Radical political liberty (press, suffrage) was not traded for other ends.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Not addressed; Manchester radicals were anti-interventionist.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Republicanism and consent doctrine favour an elected head over hereditary or indirect selection.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals disputed paper money and banking but did not address independent central banks.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Antimilitarism and anti-expansion suggest rejecting territorial absolutism; anachronistic.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Utilitarians justify property by utility, while Paine and Mill treat it as protected; split on wording.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Anachronistic twentieth-century dispute that classical radicalism never addressed.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Anachronistic environmental doctrine; utilitarian cost-benefit reasoning might oppose it, but no stance was stated.

collective-defense.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals opposed entangling military commitments yet hoped for peace.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Consent doctrine suggests yes, but not addressed.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Disestablishment and anti-clericalism suggest curbing church privilege, though disestablishment itself separates rather than subordinates.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Radicals were republicans, rejecting a symbolic hereditary head.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Consent doctrine and antimilitarism point against force.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Not addressed by the tradition; no basis to infer a view on special regional autonomy arrangements.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Paine attacks hereditary monarchy and the claim of divine origin for kings in Rights of Man (s4), which directly rejects a sacred ruler; he does not discuss divine descent in those words.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Paine's progressive scheme opposes flat rates, though income tax itself was not mainstream.

character-from-environment.rationale: Mill called education the means of forming character, and J.S. Mill stressed circumstances and education in shaping character, central to the Benthamite reform programme.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Radicals demanded accountable rulers and Paine insisted government is a creature of a constitution.

space-expansion.rationale: Anachronistic, and no radical principle bears on space as a civilizational goal.

mixed-constitution.rationale: James Mill rejected aristocracy and monarchy and favoured representation by the many.

leader-cult.rationale: The sources never discuss public veneration of a leader; opposition is inferred from radical demands for accountable government.

equal-parenting.rationale: Anachronistic family-court question; no radical position can be inferred.

land-redistribution.rationale: Paine aimed at dividing estates by taxation and abolishing primogeniture, but seizure and redistribution was only the Spencean fringe; split.

refugee-return.rationale: Not addressed by classical radicals; consent doctrine hints at sympathy but nothing was stated.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Contrary to consent doctrine and civic nationalism.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Freedom of conscience was a core radical demand, and Paine and Mill defend religious liberty (s2, s4), which excludes penalties for leaving a faith; apostasy law is not discussed directly.

women-must-cover.rationale: Compulsory dress laws are not discussed; opposition is inferred from Mill's harm principle (s3).

common-currency.rationale: Anachronistic; classical radicals debated gold and paper money, not multi-country currency unions.

worker-ownership.rationale: Collective worker ownership was an Owenite and later idea; classical radicals sought wider individual property and market enterprise, with only J.S. Mill later sympathetic to cooperatives.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Radicals wanted a limited, accountable state and cheaper government; strengthening state power for security runs against that.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Political economists of the radical circle (Ricardo, Mill) and Manchester free-traders opposed fixing prices, though radicals protested grain-price distress.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Radicals attacked aristocracy, sinecures and hereditary privilege; abolition of titles is among the positions listed for radicalism.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Not addressed; radicals favoured civic nationalism and equal rights for all, which neither requires nor rules out minority self-government, so adherents would be split.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Inferred from the radical demand for equal natural rights and civic citizenship (Paine) and the campaigns for removing religious disabilities.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Radicals believed reason, education and institutional reform drive progress, so ideas were prime movers; inferred from the rationalist Philosophic Radicals.

ban-cartels.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals hated monopolies and privilege and wanted free competition, but also distrusted state interference in the economy, so the answer is split.

no-bailouts.rationale: Inferred from laissez-faire political economy and the radical attack on sinecures and public spending for the favoured few.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Radicals wanted sovereignty in a wide electorate and distrusted aristocratic institutions, but the Mills and Paine also stressed rights and the danger of majority tyranny; adherents split.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Anachronistic; most radicals did not seek female representation, and the few who did (J.S. Mill) argued for votes not quotas, so rejection is inferred.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Radicals, especially the Manchester free-traders, campaigned against the Corn Laws and for open trade and cheap government.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the free-trade creed of Cobden and Bright, which treated trade as peaceful and unconditioned.

moral-incentives.rationale: Not addressed; the utilitarian psychology of the Philosophic Radicals took self-interest and reward as the natural motive for work.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Radicals mainly sought reform by agitation, petition and the vote; the Chartist physical-force wing was a minority, so the idea is mostly rejected.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Radicals prized rational, universal education and attacked aristocratic and national myth; a nation-centred curriculum is inferred as disfavoured, not stated.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: J.S. Mill defended tutelage of the unready, but the radical mainstream (equal natural rights, antimilitarism) opposed rule over other peoples; inferred.

patriotic-education.rationale: Radicals wanted education aimed at reason and critical citizenship and distrusted deference to crown and flag; inferred from their rationalism and antimilitarism.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Racial preferences are anachronistic; inferred from the radical demand to abolish privilege and give all equal rights regardless of birth.

public-money-creation.rationale: Chartist and Attwoodite currency reformers wanted public control of money while the Philosophic Radicals and Paine distrusted paper issues; adherents split.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Free-trade radicals such as Cobden and Bright expected commerce and growth to bring lasting prosperity; inferred, as collapse theory came later.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and sought cheaper government, so cultivating influence over a predecessor empire's lands is inferred as disfavoured.

delink-world-market.rationale: Free trade was a core radical demand, notably the Anti-Corn Law League, so cutting ties with the world market runs against it.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Anachronistic: radicals saw workers as sharing an interest against aristocratic privilege, not as beneficiaries of empire; inferred from Paine's relief proposals.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Radicals attacked legal privilege and demanded equal rights; no period statement on private discrimination, inferred from equal-rights principles tempered by Mill's liberty doctrine.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Paine championed written constitutions that bind government, but Bentham and the utilitarians rejected natural rights as a basis, so adherents were divided.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Not addressed; the period predates the modern question.

elective-rulers.rationale: Radicals, following Paine, rejected hereditary monarchy and aristocracy and wanted government by election.

minority-veto.rationale: Utilitarian radicals favoured majority rule on greatest-happiness grounds; inferred.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Paine argued that governments rest on consent and may be changed when they break trust.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The radical programme sought a wide franchise and an elected legislature as the seat of authority.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Bentham's sentience argument is a radical tradition; inferred, not in sources opened.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Utilitarian reasoning permits use with minimal suffering; inferred.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Radicals held relief as a right and attacked aristocratic privilege, not paternal duty.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Radicals campaigned for franchise, reform and public activity.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Radicals championed press freedom and public enlightenment; inferred.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Radicals relied on reason and education, and attacked ruling class corruption; inferred.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Free-trade radicals held that commerce benefits all nations; inferred.

native-born-offices.rationale: Civic nationalism and equal rights imply no birth-based exclusions; inferred.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Free-trade radicals favoured open commerce over self-reliance.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and opposed wars; inferred.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Radicals held to universal equal rights and no birth-based privileges; inferred.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from liberal commitment to equal rights.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic; liberal commitment to freedom and equal rights suggests condemning both; inferred.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Not addressed in the sources opened; left neutral as no position can be inferred from the ideology's principles.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Not addressed in the sources opened; left neutral as no position can be inferred from the ideology's principles.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Radicals held rational constitutional principles to be universal; inferred.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and opposed standing armies and military power over civil government.

filial-duty.rationale: Not addressed; radicals focused on political and legal reform, not family duties.

office-by-exam.rationale: Inferred: Benthamite radicals attacked patronage and sinecures and favoured merit-based public service, though they also wanted elected legislatures.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Inferred from the free-trade and anti-protection stance of Cobden, Bright and the Manchester radicals.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Inferred: Bentham and J.S. Mill favoured liberty in personal matters and Mill criticised the legal subjection of wives.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Radicals wanted frequent elections but not instructed delegates; Mill defended representatives' independent judgment.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Split: Paine proposed tax-funded old-age support while Manchester radicals preferred self-help and thrift.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Mainstream radicals defended private property, though Mill and some radicals backed land reform against aristocratic landed estates.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Radicals demanded cheap, accountable government and Commons control of taxation and spending against the Crown and aristocracy.

single-official-language.rationale: Not addressed as a programme; inferred indifference.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Inferred from free-trade, open-market principles; they did not discuss foreign land ownership.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Inferred: liberal radicals stressed equal formal treatment before the law; outcome-based tests of discrimination are anachronistic.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Inferred: utilitarian radicals viewed wealth and consumption as legitimate sources of welfare, though Mill criticised mere money-getting.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Cobden and Bright opposed foreign entanglements and armed intervention, though many radicals sympathised with foreign liberal movements.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Cobden and Bright championed non-intervention in other states' affairs and opposed military force abroad.

corporate-influence.rationale: Radicals attacked 'Old Corruption', the capture of government by privileged interests; corporate lobbying is a modern form, so this is inferred from that.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Inferred from the radical commitment to press freedom and free exchange; restrictions on funding would have looked like state control of opinion.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: The Mill circle were Malthusians who feared population growth outrunning wages, so they would not subsidise births; inferred, as the issue was framed differently then.

residents-only-property.rationale: Radicals attacked landed privilege and monopoly and wanted free markets in land, so local purchase bars would be seen as restrictions; inferred.

job-guarantee.rationale: The philosophic radicals backed the strict 1834 Poor Law and laissez-faire labour markets, so a state job guarantee runs against their outlook; inferred.

democratic-peace.rationale: Paine argued that representative republics would end the wars of kings, and Cobden and Bright tied free government and trade to peace.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Utilitarian radicals grounded obedience in utility rather than in a duty to law as such, so obedience is conditional; inferred from Bentham and Mill.

non-intervention.rationale: Cobden and Bright's Manchester radicals opposed foreign interventions and standing armaments, though radicals were not uniform on this.

industrial-unions.rationale: Unions were legalised in 1824 with radical help, but the industrial versus craft question is anachronistic for the period and not an issue radicals settled.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Radicals sought equal civil rights and religious toleration; their conspiracy theories targeted the aristocracy and placemen, not minorities. Inferred.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Mill's liberty doctrine and the radical law-reform tradition favoured reforming marriage law toward equal rights, not abolishing it as a legal institution; inferred.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Bentham and the philosophic radicals made publicity of government a safeguard against misrule, alongside freedom of the press.

local-production.rationale: The programme included free trade and cheaper government, which sits against a preference for mainly local production.

informal-organisation.rationale: Radicals built formal societies and leagues such as the Anti-Corn Law League and Chartist associations; inferred from their organising practice.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The question of international law versus national constitutions did not arise in this form in the period; radicals were split between legalism and sovereignty, so it is inferred as split.

religious-nation.rationale: Radicals demanded secular or disestablished churches and religious equality, which excludes defining the nation by religion.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Radicals such as Paine and Cobden opposed war and hegemony and favoured states dealing as equals; this is inferred from that anti-militarism.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Radicals wanted one national franchise and cheap government but left regional fiscal questions unaddressed; inferred as split.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Radicals defended private property and commerce and did not call for common ownership of production, so the personal/productive split is inferred as not theirs.

defeat-communism.rationale: Communism as a state system postdates the period; inferred from Cobden-style non-intervention and anti-militarism that radicals would favour coexistence.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Radicals wanted cheap, accountable government yet Benthamites also built state inspectorates; inferred as split.

religion-illusion.rationale: Radicals were secularist or nonconformist and Paine a deist, but none held religion to be a consoling illusion fading with material change; inferred.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Paine and the Manchester free-traders saw commerce and industry as engines of progress and peace, a view documented in the radical tradition.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Radicals sought legal and political equality; economic transformation for women's equality is anachronistic, though J.S. Mill's reforms-through-law approach points the same way.

socialized-care.rationale: Domestic work as a public service is a later socialist idea; radicals favoured limited, cheap government and private family arrangements.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Radicals were rationalist and universalist and no source ties them to language purism; inferred.

treaties-binding.rationale: Radical principles of consent and equal natural rights imply that agreements bind both sides; inferred, as no source addresses internal-nation treaties.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Owenite communities were a separate socialist current; mainstream radicals stressed individual rights, property and national representation.

majority-settlement.rationale: Radical civic nationalism and equal rights give no basis for steering majority settlement into minority regions; inferred.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Radicals backed commerce and free trade and the capitalism-versus-communism dichotomy is anachronistic; inferred they would reject a third way.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Inferred from Paine's universal natural rights, which ground claims in individual equality rather than historical tie to a land.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the radical commitment to reason and evidence.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Inferred from the Mills' liberty doctrine and Bentham's utilitarianism, which see no harm justifying criminal punishment of private conduct.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Radicals demanded freedom of the press and free expression, as in Paine's Rights of Man and Mill's liberty doctrine.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Radicals wanted secular or disestablished churches and, in Mill's doctrine, no punishment of opinions.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Free-trade radicals such as Cobden and Bright opposed colonial expansion as costly and aristocratic.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from their secular liberalism, which did not recognise religious obligations as politically binding.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Inferred from Paine's view that government rests on the nation and that religious authority has no claim to rule.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Radicals sought wide suffrage and frequent elections, but through representatives, not direct decisions in workplaces; inferred.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals focused on political privilege, not on the overlap of race, sex and class.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Anachronistic; Mill's liberty principle suggests tolerance but the radicals never addressed it.

assisted-dying.rationale: Inferred from Mill's principle that individuals are sovereign over themselves where others are not harmed.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Inferred: they defined themselves as the left of liberalism and saw a real divide with aristocratic privilege.

alienated-labor.rationale: Inferred: they defended private property and free markets and did not use the concept of alienation.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from their universalist liberal outlook.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Paine in Rights of Man holds that sovereignty resides in the nation and rejects government by divine right or hereditary claim.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Anachronistic; Mill's liberty favours personal choice while the secular-state tradition favours neutrality, so it is split.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from their opposition to privilege and concern for equal treatment before the law.

social-market-economy.rationale: They favoured free trade and cheap government and so opposed state-run economies, though some accepted limited reform.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: They wanted cheaper government and smaller standing armies but did not call for abolition.

rich-first.rationale: Inferred from Manchester free-trade belief that growth spreads through markets and general wealth.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Cobden and Bright championed non-intervention and opposed entanglement in great-power alliances and wars.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Paine's Rights of Man attacks hereditary government as a usurpation of the rights of later generations, and radicals demanded an end to hereditary monarchy.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Not a period issue; radicals favoured free trade and cheap government, but Owenite and Chartist co-operative credit schemes appeared on the radical fringe, so inferred.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: International lenders such as the IMF did not exist; Cobden-era radicals favoured free trade and sound public finance, so inferred as split.

property-franchise.rationale: Early radicals demanded broad or universal male suffrage, as Paine and the Chartists did, though some philosophic radicals like James Mill accepted limits; a minority position among them.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Radicals did not link women's and nature's domination; Mill later argued for women's equality but the idea is anachronistic, so inferred and a disagree.

reification.rationale: Reification is a Marxist concept from after the period; radicals defended market society and saw economic laws as natural, so inferred.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Radicals campaigned for a free, cheap press against stamp taxes and noted the influence of wealth and aristocracy, though they largely thought liberty enough, so mild agree.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Paine and Bentham demanded government by known, public laws against arbitrary rule and sinecure; legal reform and codification were central radical goals.

racial-franchise.rationale: Paine's Rights of Man rejects political distinctions of birth (s4), and radicals sought equal citizenship, which excludes an ethnic franchise; race is not discussed directly.

online-participation.rationale: The internet is anachronistic; radicals' wide participation and public opinion principles suggest favour, but this is an inference.

open-government-data.rationale: Bentham's publicity principle held that open government is a check on misrule, and radicals attacked secrecy and corruption in government.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Radicals favoured disestablishment, religious toleration and civil marriage for dissenters; they opposed legal religious restrictions.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Classical radicals demanded toleration and equal civil rights regardless of religion, as in the Mill liberty doctrine; targeting a minority conflicts with that.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the radical demand for elected, accountable legislatures on a wide franchise and secret ballot, not selection by lot.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Radicals were rationalist and anti-clerical, attacking established churches and urging that belief be tested by reason, as in Paine; they favoured rethinking inherited doctrine.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Paine proposed progressive taxes on large estates to curb aristocratic accumulation and the radicals attacked aristocratic privilege, but they accepted private property broadly.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Not an issue of the period; inferred from the radical harm principle (J.S. Mill) and rational penal reform that oppose penalizing private conduct.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Radicals sought secular or disestablished churches and freedom of conscience, not state promotion of unbelief; Paine was a deist and defended liberty of conscience.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Radicals reformed rather than abolished the penal system; Bentham designed prisons and the radicals sought rational penal reform.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Radicals wanted representation on equal individual rights and consent of the majority via wider suffrage; communal power-sharing is anachronistic, inferred.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Paine proposed state-funded poor relief and the radicals sought to replace aristocratic patronage with rational public provision, so they did not rely on charity.

term-limits.rationale: Radicals demanded frequent elections and an end to sinecures and career placemen; Paine and the Chartists urged annual parliaments, close to limits on tenure though not term limits as such.

vote-delegation.rationale: Anachronistic; the philosophic radicals favoured representative government with a wide franchise, with each person voting for themselves via the secret ballot, inferred.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals focused on present institutional reform and the greatest happiness of the living, inferred.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Radicals pressed for disestablishment but James Mill notably argued against women's suffrage, while Paine and Mill later supported women's rights; the circle was split and the specific religious-office question was not addressed.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: J.S. Mill's circle later argued marital equality, but James Mill and most radicals did not; split.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Radicals wanted the franchise widened to citizens; the question of resident non-citizens voting was not addressed, so this is left neutral.

rent-control.rationale: Radicals of the Manchester school and philosophic radicals favoured free markets and cheap government, so price-setting by the state is inferred as disliked.

abolish-ip.rationale: Bentham and the Mills accepted patents as a reward for invention, though they disliked monopolies; abolition is inferred as not their position.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Radicals attacked standing armies and militarism as instruments of aristocratic government, so drilled national-service youth movements are inferred as opposed.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Nuclear weapons postdate the movement; its general anti-militarism points slightly one way but adherents cannot be placed, so this is neutral.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Cobden and Bright urged non-intervention and avoiding foreign entanglements and military establishments, from which a dislike of foreign bases is inferred.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Radicals condemned oppression and atrocity on humanitarian grounds, so formal recognition is inferred as mildly agreeable; the issue is anachronistic.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Radicals attacked sinecures, aristocratic privilege and unearned rents, and Mill criticised income from mere ownership of land.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Most utilitarian and liberal radicals accepted force in self-defence; only a Quaker-influenced minority held absolute non-killing.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Paine rejected appeals to ancient inheritance and the radicals argued from reason and rights rather than national origins; inferred from that.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Radicals were rationalists who treated social arrangements as open to reform, but sex as socially constructed is anachronistic, so this is inferred.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: The issue is anachronistic; radicals' universalist rights language neither supports nor opposes the claim.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Rationalist and utilitarian radicals disliked glorifying death for the nation as military and aristocratic sentiment, and sacralising it more so.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Radicals argued politics on utility, reason and rights, often with secular or disestablishmentarian leanings, so a good-versus-evil spiritual war is inferred as foreign to them.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: The diaspora-centre idea postdates radicalism and its universalism gives no clear lead.

culture-before-state.rationale: Radicals focused on reforming government and the state first (franchise, ballot, legal reform) rather than a cultural renewal.

god-not-male.rationale: Many radicals were freethinkers or dissenters, but the question of divine gender was not addressed by the movement.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Mill later wrote for women's equality, but radicals as a whole took no common line on judging scripture.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Radicals favoured free trade and equal rights regardless of birth and opposed privileged groups, so reserving economic life for a national majority is inferred as opposed.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Radical reform concerned equal representation and constituency reform by population, not merging regions by people; inferred.

independent-unions.rationale: Inferred: radicals pressed for repeal of the Combination Acts and freedom of association; independence from the state follows from their distrust of government.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Inferred: radicals sought political reform and free markets, not working-class socialism.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Inferred: they reformed municipal government but the sources opened do not address public ownership of essentials.

second-chamber.rationale: Radicals attacked the hereditary House of Lords and aristocratic privilege, so a second chamber was suspect.

municipal-property.rationale: Inferred: they defended private property and free trade, not community ownership of production.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Inferred: the Chartists and radicals favoured a strong elected parliament; no stated view on confederations.

family-wage.rationale: Inferred: no position on wage levels; free-market radicals mostly left wages to the market.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Anachronistic; liberty and press freedom point one way, hard-money views another.

online-anonymity.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from radical defence of press freedom and anonymous political pamphleteering.

person-over-state.rationale: Mill's liberty doctrine and Paine's rights of man make the individual's rights prior to state ends.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Inferred: radicals ranged from the secular Benthamites to dissenting Christians, so adherents split.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Inferred: not an issue for them; reformers favoured both local and central reform.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Inferred: radicals stressed individual rights and universal principles rather than group interests.

racial-pride.rationale: Inferred: the sources opened do not address race, and period views varied.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Cobden and Bright championed peace, non-intervention and cheaper government, opposing aggressive wars.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Radicals were largely universalist and focused on franchise and institutions; national-linguistic identity was not a defining issue, so inferred and neutral.

communal-electorates.rationale: Radicals demanded equal individual citizenship and a uniform wide franchise; inferred from the Chartist and Mill suffrage demands, which oppose sectional representation.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Radicals attacked the aristocratic state rather than fearing foreign plots, and Paine was cosmopolitan; inferred from The Rights of Man.

free-public-college.rationale: Radicals favoured cheap government and expanded education, but free university tuition was not in the programme; inferred and split.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Philosophic radicals favoured free markets and minimal taxation of trade; inferred from laissez-faire and cheap government.

future-generations.rationale: Utilitarian concern for general welfare could extend to posterity, but this was not stated; inferred from Bentham and Mill.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Radicals argued from universal individual rights and utility, not gender difference; inferred from Mill's liberty doctrine.

arms-reduction.rationale: Radicals demanded cheap government and opposed standing armies and military expenditure; Cobden and Bright campaigned for retrenchment and peace.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Radicals attacked secret diplomacy as aristocratic; Cobden and Bright demanded open foreign policy and publicity.

capital-controls.rationale: Radicals championed free trade and free commerce; Cobden and the Manchester school opposed state interference with trade and capital.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Radicals were split: they favoured citizen militias over standing armies, but also backed order against mobs, and the sources opened do not settle this.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Inferred: Paine and the radicals opposed war as a tool of monarchs but did not endorse soldiers refusing orders.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Inferred: philosophic radicals and Manchester liberals favoured free contract and laissez-faire, though combination laws were repealed with radical support.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Inferred: Benthamite radicals opposed wage subsidies such as the Speenhamland system, favouring self-reliance and the reformed Poor Law.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Inferred: radicals demanded cheap, retrenched government and low taxes, which fits limits on borrowing.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Inferred: radicals backed free trade among nations on equal terms, not rules tilted to developing countries.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Inferred: radicals sought parliamentary reform through franchise extension and the ballot, not destruction of the state, though Paine defended revolution against the old regime.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Inferred: radical political economy held firm principles of free trade and free markets rather than varied community experimentation.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Inferred: pre-ecological liberalism treated nature as private property, and a modern capital-valuation idea was not in view.

sacred-nation.rationale: Radicals were rationalist and cosmopolitan; Paine's Rights of Man rejects mystic inherited authority and treats the nation as a society of equal citizens.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Inferred: no mass student lending existed, and radical self-reliance and limited government cut against debt cancellation.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Inferred: radicals attacked aristocratic privilege rather than regional exploitation, though Irish grievances were sometimes raised.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Paine's Rights of Man grounds equal natural rights in the unity and common creation of all people (s4); whether human nature should be redesigned is not discussed.

public-service-media.rationale: Inferred: radicals demanded freedom of the press from state control and taxation but did not propose state-funded media.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Inferred from Paine's deism and the radical push for toleration and disestablishment, which treated religions as varieties of a shared reason-based faith; not a stated demand.

farm-price-support.rationale: Inferred from the free-trade, laissez-faire radicalism of Cobden and Bright, which opposed the Corn Laws and state-managed prices.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: The question is anachronistic for the period, and nothing in the sources bears on it.

workers-own-party.rationale: Radicals led parliamentary reform, and Chartists demanded a wider franchise rather than a class party, so the demand for a separate workers' party is not one this mainstream held.

ban-fgm.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the utilitarian and rational legal reform that would ban a harmful practice by law.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Inferred from the radical attack on aristocratic privilege and Paine's hostility to primogeniture; the Mills' own views on women were mixed.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Anachronistic and not addressed in the sources.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Inferred from the liberal tort-and-property approach and Mill's harm principle, which holds that harm to others is the ground for liability; the period had no agency regulation.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: The radicals attacked hereditary and aristocratic privilege and demanded representation by elected government, so a formal role for traditional leaders is the opposite of their programme.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from Mill's liberty doctrine and the harm principle, which limit liberty only for harm to others.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Penal reform on rational or utilitarian grounds, as Bentham argued, favoured calibrating punishment to the case and cutting excessive fixed penalties like capital offences.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Anachronistic; the radicals favoured education but mass migration policy was not in their programme.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Radical liberalism stressed freedom of contract and association, and repealed the Combination Acts; opposition to compulsion is inferred, not stated.

voter-id.rationale: Radicals wanted the widest possible franchise; voter ID was anachronistic, so this is an inference from that aim.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Radicals sought disestablishment and an end to the privileges of the established church.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Radicals centred reform on frequent, competitive elections and the secret ballot, though J.S. Mill also worried about majority tyranny; adherents leaned procedural.

premarital-sex.rationale: Adherents were split: Bentham and Mill were permissive on sexual morality, but Victorian moral reformers also sat among the radicals.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from their strong commitment to freedom of the press and suspicion of government power.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Anachronistic; radicals favored cheap government and the harsh 1834 Poor Law reform but nothing like a cash-transfer scheme, so this is inferred.

women-suffrage.rationale: J.S. Mill and Bentham argued for votes for women, though James Mill disagreed, so the radical mainstream was split but leaned in favor.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Radicals criticized established churches as a source of privilege but did not call religion a main cause of women's oppression; inferred.

race-social-construct.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from universalist, anti-slavery rationalism in the radical tradition.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from their preference for small, cheap government.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Adherents were split: Lockean-leaning radicals accepted ownership by labour, while Paine treated the earth as common property.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Inferred from the philosophic radicals' rationalist internationalism (Bentham proposed an international court for peace); ICCs themselves are anachronistic.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Inferred from Paine's deism and the radicals' secularism and rationalism; nonconformist radicals were split on scripture.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Inferred from the equal-rights principle of Bentham and the Mills; the question itself is anachronistic.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Radicals championed free trade, cheap government and a slimmed-down executive, opposed to state-run planned economies.

indirect-election.rationale: They demanded a wide direct franchise, the secret ballot and frequent elections, not election by intermediate bodies.

national-church-status.rationale: Disestablishment of the Church of England and equality of religious bodies were central radical and nonconformist demands.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Inferred from their civic nationalism and equal-law outlook; they did not address ethnic territorial autonomy.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Inferred from Paine's principle of government by consent of the governed; plebiscites were not a developed radical doctrine.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Anachronistic: radicals criticised empire (Cobden, Bentham) but did not address inherited borders after independence.

simple-living.rationale: Inferred from their commitment to commerce, free trade and material improvement, which favour abundance over limited needs.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Inferred from the liberty principle and free movement of people and trade; they did not address indigenous homelands.

equal-conscription.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and opposed standing armies, and J.S. Mill argued for sexual equality; inferred, as conscription of women was not discussed.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Radicals grounded politics in rights, consent and reason rather than ancestral bonds, though civic nationalism was part of the movement; inferred.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Penal reform on rational grounds and rights against arbitrary power imply that the state may not kill without trial; Paine and the Benthamites demanded legal process.

close-ties-china.rationale: China relations are anachronistic for this period; free trade with all nations would apply, but there is no stated position.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Radical antimilitarism and distrust of foreign entanglements imply against state sponsorship of kin abroad; inferred.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Paine proposed poor relief and a progressive estate tax so wealth owed to the community is shared, which supports the idea, though compensation for resource appropriation is inferred.

self-ownership.rationale: J.S. Mill's liberty doctrine and the radical emphasis on equal natural rights supports personal sovereignty over body and labour.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: The Anti-Corn Law League attacked taxes on bread and other food and radicals demanded cheaper government and lower taxation.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Utilitarian poor-law reformers favoured relief aimed at the destitute; Paine's proposals also targeted the poor. Inferred, as universal provision was not on the agenda.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Radicals demanded a wider franchise and representative government; they sought to empower parties and the electorate, not a leader outside them, and rejected hereditary rule.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Radicals attacked sinecures, aristocratic privilege and monopolies, and the Corn Laws as a landowner privilege.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Disestablishment of churches and secularism were radical aims, which opposes denominationally organised politics.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Rationalist progress and reform rather than return to tradition marks the radicals; inferred.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: J.S. Mill and others argued for women's equality in marriage law, but the wider radical movement was mixed and the issue is only inferred.

national-resource-control.rationale: Free trade and open commerce were central, so exclusive national control over resources is inferred as unwelcome.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Inferred: radicals attacked unearned privilege and aristocratic property but also defended commercial property and free exchange, and adherents were split.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the radicals' commitment to free trade and opposition to taxes on commerce.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Anachronistic question; radicals opposed slavery but the post-civil-rights framing of the statement was unknown to them.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: The philosophic radicals followed Bentham and James Mill's utilitarianism, which rejects natural law; law was judged by its consequences, though Paine's natural rights stood opposed.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Anachronistic; Mill anticipated a stationary state and shorter work in time, but the radicals did not address automation.

multipolar-world.rationale: Inferred: Cobden and Bright opposed balance-of-power diplomacy and imperial entanglements in favour of non-intervention and trade between independent nations.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Inferred: Ricardian and Mill-era classical economics, which radicals adopted, grounded value largely in labour and cost of production.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Inferred: Paine and the Chartists appealed to the people and their rights against aristocratic rule, joining national feeling with the interests of ordinary workers.

material-over-identity.rationale: Anachronistic: the radicals' concern was franchise and privilege, and the left's later dispute over cultural identity did not exist.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Inferred: the radicals were liberals committed to private enterprise and representative government, with no communist party or socialist system.

missingStatements.text: Seats in the legislature should be filled by a wide franchise of ordinary citizens, not limited to property owners.
missingStatements.rationale: Extension of the franchise was the defining radical demand, argued by Bentham, the Mills and the Chartists.

missingStatements.text: Voting should be by secret ballot.
missingStatements.rationale: James Mill's 1830 essay The Ballot defended secret voting as protection against intimidation, and radical pressure led to the Ballot Act 1872.
missingStatements.declined: Settled in every modern democracy; no ideology in the bank would take the opposite side, so it fails the contested test.

missingStatements.text: Hereditary titles and privileges should be abolished.
missingStatements.rationale: Radicals attacked aristocracy, sinecures and hereditary privilege; abolition of titles is among the positions listed for radicalism.

notes: Strands differ: Paine and Chartists were more egalitarian and sympathetic to force, philosophic radicals were utilitarian and constitutional, and Manchester radicals prioritised free trade and cheap government. Several answers are split for that reason. Statement ids with no period analogue are low-confidence inferences.
